abstract: Pioneer transcription factors bind nucleosomal DNA and establish accessible chromatin, yet their binding is tissue specific. While studies have largely focused on protein-extrinsic features, like chromatin structure and cofactor expression, the mechanisms governing the tissue-specific binding remain poorly understood. We used the Drosophila pioneer transcription factor Zelda as a paradigm to investigate the mechanisms controlling tissue-specific binding. Zelda promotes the undifferentiated state in both the embryo and in neural stem cells of the larval brain. However, Zelda binds thousands of unique sites in each tissue and, in so doing, defines tissue-specific enhancers. We showed that tissue-specific binding is controlled by the developmentally regulated use of two distinct DNA-binding domains. Our identification of a novel, neural stem cell enriched Zelda proteoform that lacks the embryo-specific C-terminal DNA-binding domain explains the differential DNA-binding domain usage. This proteoform arises through developmentally regulated -1 ribosomal frameshifting, a mechanism common to viruses but not documented for any eukaryotic transcription factors. Together we revealed a new strategy where developmentally programmed ribosomal frameshifting confers tissue-specific pioneer-factor binding and suggest that this mechanism may be more broadly used to diversify the proteome than previously appreciated.
